clinicalPearls: MAT is defined by an irregular atrial tachycardia with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and varying PP, PR and RR intervals at a rate above 100 per minute.
It is strongly associated with decompensated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other causes of hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension.
An isoelectric baseline between clearly discernible P waves distinguishes MAT from atrial fibrillation, which lacks organised atrial activity.
Other precipitants include theophylline toxicity, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, sepsis and the postoperative state.
Treatment centres on correcting the underlying pulmonary and metabolic disturbance rather than on antiarrhythmic drugs.
Magnesium and potassium repletion can reduce ectopy even when baseline levels appear within the reference range.
Beta-blockers are effective for rate control but are frequently limited by bronchospastic disease, so a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker is often preferred.
Direct-current cardioversion is ineffective because the mechanism is enhanced automaticity from multiple foci rather than reentry.
reference.pathophysiology: MAT results from abnormal automaticity or triggered activity arising from multiple ectopic atrial foci, producing P waves of differing morphology and timing. It typically occurs in the setting of atrial stretch, hypoxaemia, catecholamine excess and metabolic derangement, conditions epitomised by decompensated chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with right atrial enlargement and elevated pulmonary pressures. Fluctuating autonomic tone, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and drugs such as theophylline and beta-agonists further destabilise atrial membrane potentials and promote ectopic firing. Because the arrhythmia is driven by automatic foci rather than a fixed reentrant circuit, it does not respond to cardioversion and resolves chiefly with correction of the underlying disturbance.
additionalDifferentials: frequent atrial premature complexes with wandering atrial pacemaker
sinus tachycardia with premature atrial beats
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG demonstrating three or more P-wave morphologies with an isoelectric baseline
arterial blood gas analysis to assess hypoxaemia and acid-base status
theophylline level where the drug is in use
chest imaging to evaluate underlying pulmonary disease
echocardiography to assess right heart size, pulmonary pressures and left ventricular function
redFlags: severe hypoxaemia or respiratory failure driving the arrhythmia
haemodynamic instability from a rapid ventricular response
features of decompensated cor pulmonale or right heart failure
reference.prognosis: MAT itself is rarely dangerous, but it signals serious underlying illness and its prognosis reflects the severity of the associated pulmonary or systemic disease. The arrhythmia usually resolves once the precipitating condition is treated.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing MAT as atrial fibrillation and pursuing rate or rhythm strategies aimed at the wrong mechanism.
Attempting electrical cardioversion, which does not work for an automatic multifocal rhythm.
Prescribing non-selective beta-blockers in bronchospastic disease and worsening respiratory status.
Overlooking magnesium deficiency because the serum level appears normal.
Focusing on antiarrhythmic therapy while neglecting the underlying hypoxaemia and metabolic derangement.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with supraventricular tachycardia
management: Treat the underlying precipitant by correcting hypoxaemia and optimising decompensated COPD with bronchodilators and treatment of infection
Correct metabolic derangement with magnesium and potassium repletion, which reduces atrial ectopy
Review and reduce arrhythmogenic drugs, particularly theophylline and beta-agonists
Rate control with a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as verapamil or diltiazem, reserving beta-blockers for those without significant bronchospasm
Avoid direct-current cardioversion, which is ineffective against an automatically driven, non-reentrant rhythm
Monitor with continuous ECG and repeat electrolytes, escalating care according to the severity of the underlying pulmonary or systemic illness
